analysis.one_liner: Lets gun violence victims sue gun makers and sellers for negligence, ending the industry's special legal shield.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill; it died at the end of the 113th Congress without a floor vote, backed by 25 House members, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people injured by guns, or their families, sue gun manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations for negligence or defective products, even when a criminal pulled the trigger. It targeted a 2005 law that shields the gun industry from most such lawsuits, and it would have made federal gun-trace records usable as evidence in court. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would gain the same right to sue for negligence or defective design that people injured by any other product have. They could also use federal gun-trace data as evidence to show that a particular dealer or maker negligently supplied crime guns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Courts could no longer dismiss negligence or product-defect suits against gun manufacturers, sellers, or trade associations merely because the harm involved a criminal or unlawful use of the gun [S2][S3].

The ATF's Firearms Trace System database would become subject to subpoena and admissible as evidence in civil suits, on the same basis as other information, letting plaintiffs document patterns of negligent sales [S2][S3].

The bill's findings argue the protection is narrow in practice: it states that 86% of dealers sell no guns later used in crimes, while 1.2% of dealers account for 57% of crime guns, so most law-abiding sellers would face little new exposure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations, which would face negligence and defect lawsuits and the litigation costs that come with them, and could pass some of those costs to buyers through higher prices or required liability insurance. Small dealers selling lawfully could still be named in suits and bear legal defense costs even if they ultimately win.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Even responsible small dealers could be drawn into costly litigation over criminal acts by third parties, since suits could proceed to discovery before any negligence was established [S2].

The 2005 law the bill would override was enacted to protect a lawful industry from suits designed to run it down through the courts; critics argue that civil litigation is the wrong tool for harms caused by criminals who misuse a legal product [S2][S3].
Liability exposure and insurance costs could raise prices for lawful gun buyers, an effect the bill does not address [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give gun violence victims the same access to civil remedies as victims of any other defective or negligently sold product, and the bill's own findings concede the exemption is unique among American industries. The main cost is litigation risk for gun sellers, though the findings indicate the burden would fall mostly on the small share of dealers tied to most crime guns. The trade-off is real but modest for responsible sellers; the biggest losers would be the industry's broad legal immunity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on January 22, 2013, joined by 11 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
All 24 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations kept the 2005 law that shields them from most negligence and defect lawsuits, and gun violence victims gained no new access to the courts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers kept their liability shield

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give gun violence victims the same civil remedies as other product-injury victims

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats, none were Republicans

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; controlled the markup schedule
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two years before the Congress ended, keeping it from any vote

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.role: Gun rights lobby that backed the 2005 industry liability law
against.what_they_did: Supported keeping the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act and opposed legislation reopening gun industry lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican joined [S4]; the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill [S5].

industries.industry: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill would strip the industry's unique shield from negligence and product-defect lawsuits and make federal trace data usable against it in court. Its interest in keeping that immunity runs directly against victims' access to the courts.
New lawsuit exposure for sellers would increase demand for liability coverage, though the bill itself does not address insurance.
